By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Has South Africa’s squeaky clean image as host nation of the 2010 Soccer World Cup been tarnished forever?

Summary:
FIFA, the organisation that governs professional soccer in 209 countries under the watchful eye of Sepp Blatter, who was re-elected as President for a fifth term last Friday, have been dogged by bribery and corruption for many years.
On Wednesday, it's probably been dealt it biggest blow.
In 24 dramatic hours this week, the game has fundamentally changed for FIFA with the release of an indictment by the US Attorney General of charges of bribery, racketeering and corruption. The charges involve tens of millions of US dollars and date back to 1991.





Further information:
At dawn on Wednesday morning, Swiss Police arrested seven top-officials on behalf of the FBI – including FIFA vice-presidents, Jeffrey Webb and Eugenio Figueredo. More arrests followed, with 14 FIFA officials implicated in the US’s 164-page indictment. They all face extradition from Switzerland.

In Miami, FBI agents raided the offices of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football.
And two South Africans are also implicated by the indictment.

The US indictment claims that two “high ranking officials of the 2006 and 2010 South Africa World Cup bid committees and the local organising committee” were involved in paying bribes to influence the outcome of bids. Sports Minister, Fikile Mbalula was quick to deny these allegations.

There are two references to South Africa in the indictment. The first one claims that a high-ranking South African bid committee handed over a brief case containing ten thousand dollar stacks to a representative of Jack Warner.

The indictment states this happened in the early 2000s at a hotel in Paris, but another deal was allegedly struck in 2004.

It is then alleged that FIFA, the South Afgricvan government and the South African bid committee were prepared to arrange for an amount of ten million US dollars to be paid from the South African government to support the African diaspora.

According to the indictment, the offer would be in exchange for Warner and the two other co-conspirators’ votes in favour of South Africa.
The indictment also claims that the South African government was unable to pay that money from South African funds. So, FIFA paid over the ten million US dollars which they then shaved off which they were supposed to have paid South Africa in support of the World Cup.

US and Swiss prosecutors have suggested there may be more arrests to come.

FIFAGATE SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK

Moscow, Russia…

Historical Russian Emperors and Soviet strongholds; the Kremlin, St Basil’s Cathedral, the Red Square and the Bolshoi…

But in the shadows of these landmarks in this picturesque city, lurks the Russian Mafia - one of the most structured criminal organisations in the world, their influence stretching into Western Europe, the US and beyond.

But – how is organised crime operating from Moscow’s underworld linked to the most played and watched game in the world?

(google earth) – zoom out from Moscow and into Zurich… FIFA head quarters

Zurich, Switzerland…

The headquarters of FIFA: the organisation that governs professional soccer in 209 countries under the watchful eye of Sepp Blatter, who was re-elected as President for a fifth term last Friday.
It’s in this building where just 24 officials have the power to fulfil or destroy the hopes of a nation. They decide who will host FIFA’s World Cup tournaments.

THOMAS KWENAITE: They say football is the opium of the masses. Football is played and watched by more people in more countries than all sporting games put together.

Supersport anchor, Thomas Kwe-na-i-te, has been a sports journalist for the past 23 years and has closely followed the developments at FIFA.

THOMAS KWENAITE: A lot of people have been saying something is not right within Fifa. If you have an organisation that consist of 209 members and yet the power to award such a lucrative, magnitude event lies in 24 members… This whole system is open to abuse.

For many years, FIFA’s been dogged by allegations of corruption and bribery…

DEVI LINK: The story goes back to December 2010 when Russia and Qatar won the rights to host the 2018 and 2022 World Cups. At the time, the allegations of vote rigging and bribery resurfaced, so, in a bid to clean up their image, FIFA appointed well-known American attorney, Michael Garcia to head-up an investigation.

Garcia handed his 450-page report to FIFA in November last year, but it was reduced to a 40-page summary. He appealed against the decision not to release the entire report but it was dismissed and Garcia resigned in December.

JONTY MARK: They still haven’t released the whole report, so the people can actually see what mr Garcia was saying. They still say they are going to release it in due course and they still haven’t released it.

Citizen football editor, Jonty Mark, has been a sports journalist for 15 years. He says Garcia’s resignation should point to something sinister.

JONTY MARK: We can deduce that he certainly said more than FIFA are letting on, it seems that there is some credit around the allegations of bribery and corruption.

Since the decision in 2010 to award the 2018 and 2022 tournaments to Russia and Qatar respectively, FIFA has been requested to re-vote.
Earlier this week, the Swiss authorities announced that they had also opened a criminal inquiry into these decisions.

But on Wednesday FIFA was probably dealt its biggest blow.

DEVI LINK: In just 24 dramatic hours this week, the game has fundamentally changed for FIFA with the release of an indictment by the US Attorney General which makes claims of bribery, corruption and racketeering.

The charges involve tens of millions of US dollars and date back to 1991.

LORETTA LYNCH/US ATTORNEY GENERAL (NEW YORK CITY; WEDNESDAY 27 MAY 2015): In short, these individuals, through these organisations, engaged in bribery to decide who would televise games, where the games would be held, and who would run the organisation overseeing organised soccer worldwide

An FBI-investigation that reportedly originated in Russia on an organised crime case in 2010… and whistle-blowing by US FIFA-representative, Chuck Blazer – who has subsequently turned state witness - lead to a four-year investigation into the alleged shady dealings of FIFA officials and soccer stakeholders around the world.

(zoom out of FIFA head quarters to Baur au Lac Hotel, Zurich)

At dawn on Wednesday morning, Swiss Police arrested seven top-officials on behalf of the FBI – including FIFA vice-presidents, Jeffrey Webb and Eugenio Figueredo.

More arrests followed, with 14 FIFA officials implicated in the US’s 164-page indictment. They all face extradition from Switzerland.

DAVID LOXTON: ENS AFRICA: DIRECTOR: The USA have extradition treaty with countries all around the world, including Switzerland and they would then be entitled to request the Swiss authorities to basically ship those people across to the USA to face the charges.

Attorney David Loxton says the US foreign corrupt practices act allows them wide authority to bring cases against foreign nationals living abroad.

DAVID LOXTON: So the US authorities essentially state that we have jurisdiction over you if you have had one meeting on our soil to plan your corruption, if any of your emails went through an Apple server, if you had used any banks to transfer money from the US or into the US, we have jurisdiction.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, however, called the US investigation a blatant attempt to extend US jurisdiction to other states.

(zoom out of Zurich and go to Miami)

[text: MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, USA]

Also on Wednesday, across the Atlantic Ocean in Miami, FBI agents raided the offices of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football.

(zoom out of Miami to Johannesburg, South Africa)

[TEXT: JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA]

South Africa – US authorities are also probing the awarding of Africa’s first World Cup in 2010.

DEVI LINK: There is no denying the fact that the 2010 Soccer World Cup was a resounding success. Despite the controversies, South Africans united and we proved to the world that we could pull it off.

The US indictment claims that two “high ranking officials of the 2006 and 2010 South Africa World Cup bid committees and the local organising committee” were involved in paying bribes to influence the outcome of bids.

But Sports Minister, Fikile Mbalula was quick to deny these allegations.

FIKILE MBALULA/SPORTS MINISTER: There’s nothing on our side that can implicate our government.

The indictment calls the two South Africans, co-conspirator 15 and 16 and names former FIFA vice-President – Jack Warner – as the link to them. Warner was also arrested and charged this week.

JACK WARNER: During my time at Fifa, I always conducted myself consistent, with the best international activity.

DEVI LINK: There are two references to South Africa in the indictment. The first one claims that a high-ranking South African bid committee member handed over a brief case containing ten thousand dollar stacks to a representative of Jack Warner.

The indictment states this happened in the early 2000s at a hotel in Paris, but another deal was allegedly struck in 2004.

DEVI LINK: It is then alleged that FIFA, the South African government and the South African bid committee were prepared to arrange for an amount of ten million US dollars to be paid from the South African government to support the African diaspora.

According to the indictment, the offer would be in exchange for Warner and the two other co-conspirators’ votes in favour of South Africa.

DEVI LINK: The indictment also claims that the South African government was unable to pay that money using government funds. So, FIFA paid over the ten million US dollars which they then shaved off which they were supposed to have paid South Africa in support of the World Cup.

Answering questions from reporters at a news conference in Zurich yesterday, re-elected President Sepp Blatter denied that he was the unnamed official who authorised the ten million dollar payment.

In Johannesburg on Thursday, Sports Minister, Fikile Mbalula questioned the manner in which US officials released the details of their investigation.

FIKILE MBALULA: The same as they go to Switzerland in terms of collaboration and arrested people, we too must be respected.

DEVI LINK: We requested an interview with SAFA and their spokesperson told us that he had been instructed not to talk to the media.

Blatter questioned the timing of the investigation, saying FIFA “could have been contacted at another time.”

THOMAS: If the FBI says all this has been going dating back to 1991 and Sepp Blatter is unaware of what have been going on for 24 years. You know, I start to wonder what kind of a leader is that?

US and Swiss prosecutors have suggested there may be more arrests to come. The Hawks haven’t been asked to assist with any local investigations.

How much has South Africa’s image of hosting a successful World Cup - been tarnished?

JONTY MARK: We would liked to have hosted a clean World Cup that we won faily. But then there is the argument: Is any World Cup won fairly?

metadata.Further information: At dawn on Wednesday morning, Swiss Police arrested seven top-officials on behalf of the FBI – including FIFA vice-presidents, Jeffrey Webb and Eugenio Figueredo. More arrests followed, with 14 FIFA officials implicated in the US’s 164-page indictment. They all face extradition from Switzerland. In Miami, FBI agents raided the offices of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football. And two South Africans are also implicated by the indictment. The US indictment claims that two “high ranking officials of the 2006 and 2010 South Africa World Cup bid committees and the local organising committee” were involved in paying bribes to influence the outcome of bids. Sports Minister, Fikile Mbalula was quick to deny these allegations. There are two references to South Africa in the indictment. The first one claims that a high-ranking South African bid committee handed over a brief case containing ten thousand dollar stacks to a representative of Jack Warner. The indictment states this happened in the early 2000s at a hotel in Paris, but another deal was allegedly struck in 2004. It is then alleged that FIFA, the South Afgricvan government and the South African bid committee were prepared to arrange for an amount of ten million US dollars to be paid from the South African government to support the African diaspora. According to the indictment, the offer would be in exchange for Warner and the two other co-conspirators’ votes in favour of South Africa. The indictment also claims that the South African government was unable to pay that money from South African funds. So, FIFA paid over the ten million US dollars which they then shaved off which they were supposed to have paid South Africa in support of the World Cup. US and Swiss prosecutors have suggested there may be more arrests to come.
